19288:
What it says: those who die unrepentant will exist forever under God's just judgment, consciously experiencing loss and punishment, cut off from the joy of God's presence. Many defenders today stress that the core of hell is separation from God and the self-chosen ruin of a life turned away from him, while still taking the fire imagery seriously. This is the historic majority view of Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, taught by Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin and Jonathan Edwards, and stated in confessions such as the Athanasian Creed and the Westminster Confession.

Main arguments: Jesus places 'eternal punishment' alongside 'eternal life' (Matt 25:46). Revelation says the smoke of torment 'goes up forever and ever' and the devil, beast and false prophet are 'tormented day and night forever and ever' (Rev 14:10-11, Rev 20:10). Jesus speaks of an undying worm and unquenchable fire (Mark 9:48). Sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious, and the wicked may continue to sin and refuse God forever.

Critiques: an endless punishment for sins done in a finite life seems disproportionate; Revelation 20:10 names the devil, beast and false prophet, not humans in general; and the 'forever' smoke echoes Old Testament images for a city destroyed once and for all (Isa 34:9-10). Replies: the seriousness of sin depends on whom it is against, not how long it took; Revelation 14:11 does concern humans who worship the beast; and the human and devilish fates share the same lake of fire (Matt 25:41).
19289: Straw man: 'Believers in eternal torment think God enjoys torturing people.' Correction: its serious defenders say God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11), that hell is the just consequence of refusing God, and that its worst aspect is loss of God, not a torture chamber run by demons.
19291:
What it says: humans are not immortal by nature; eternal life is God's gift given in Christ. The unrepentant will be raised, judged and punished in proportion to their sins, and then will finally cease to exist: the 'second death'. Defenders often call it 'conditional immortality' because immortality is conditional on union with Christ. Early writers such as Justin (on one reading), Theophilus and Arnobius are cited for it. Modern defenders include Edward Fudge, John Stott (cautiously, in *Essentials*, 1988), Clark Pinnock, John Stackhouse and the Rethinking Hell project.

Main arguments: only God 'has immortality' (1 Tim 6:16) and believers 'seek' it (Rom 2:7); the Bible's most common words for the fate of the wicked are death, destruction and perishing (John 3:16, Rom 6:23, Matt 10:28, Phil 3:19); God can 'destroy both soul and body in Gehenna' (Matt 10:28); the wicked become ashes and are 'no more' (Mal 4:1-3, Ps 37:10, Ps 37:20); Sodom's 'eternal fire' destroyed the cities, it did not keep burning (Jude 1:7, 2 Pet 2:6). The unquenchable fire and undying worm of Isaiah 66:24 consume corpses, not living people.

Critiques: it seems to weaken the 'eternal punishment' contrast of Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11 and 20:10 speak of torment with 'no rest day or night'; and the view has sometimes been linked to groups outside historic orthodoxy. Replies: the punishment is eternal in its result, as 'eternal destruction' (2 Thess 1:9) shows; Revelation's imagery is symbolic, drawing on Isaiah 34; and the view is now held by many orthodox evangelicals and has early patristic precedent.
19292: Straw man: 'Annihilationists believe the wicked just die and get off lightly, with no judgment.' Correction: conditionalists teach a real resurrection to judgment and punishment proportionate to sin before final destruction. They see permanent loss of existence and of God as the ultimate penalty, not an escape.
19294:
What it says: God will finally reconcile every person to himself through Christ. Hell is real, but it is a purifying, corrective fire, not endless; people may suffer long and severely, but no one is beyond God's love forever. Early defenders include Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, and Isaac the Syrian expressed a similar hope. Modern defenders include Thomas Talbott, Robin Parry and David Bentley Hart. It is distinct from pluralism, the idea that all religions are equally valid; Christian universalists hold that everyone is saved through Christ.

Main arguments: God 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Tim 2:4) and is 'the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe' (1 Tim 4:10); 'as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive' (1 Cor 15:22); God will reconcile all things (Col 1:20) and be 'all in all' (1 Cor 15:28); every tongue will confess Jesus as Lord (Phil 2:10-11); the gates of the new Jerusalem are never shut (Rev 21:25); God does not cast off forever (Lam 3:31-33). Philosophically, they argue that a perfectly loving and all-powerful God would not allow any creature to be lost forever, and that endless punishment serves no good end.

Critiques: it seems to contradict texts of final, unending judgment (Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9); it may override human freedom; it was condemned in 543 and 553 (see 'The Restoration of All Things'); and it risks removing urgency from the call to repent. Replies: universalists read *aiōnios* as 'of the age to come'; they argue freedom is fulfilled, not overridden, when people see God clearly; they dispute the scope of the sixth-century condemnations; and they point out that Gregory of Nyssa and others preached repentance fervently.
19295: Straw man: 'Universalists think sin does not matter and everyone goes straight to heaven.' Correction: Christian universalists usually hold that sin is grievous, that judgment is real and may be terrible, and that salvation comes only through Christ. They differ on whether judgment ends in restoration.
19297:
Christians agree that the final hope is to be with God in perfect joy. They differ in how they describe it.

The 'heaven as destination' emphasis focuses on the vision of God: the pure in heart 'shall see God' (Matt 5:8), 'we shall see him as he is' (1 John 3:2), 'now face to face' (1 Cor 13:12). Believers have an inheritance 'kept in heaven' (1 Pet 1:4), a 'better country, that is, a heavenly one' (Heb 11:16), and rooms in the Father's house (John 14:2-3). This picture shaped classic Catholic and Protestant teaching on the beatific vision.

The 'new creation' emphasis focuses on bodily resurrection and a renewed world: creation set free (Rom 8:19-23), new heavens and new earth (Isa 65:17, 2 Pet 3:13), and the holy city coming down so that God dwells with people (Rev 21:1-3). Heaven, on this view, is where God's future is kept now, before it comes to earth (Col 3:1-4, Phil 3:20-21).

Most traditions combine these in two stages: at death believers go to be with Christ (Phil 1:23, Luke 23:43, 2 Cor 5:8), the 'intermediate state'; at Christ's return they are raised bodily for life in the new creation, where they see God face to face (Rev 22:3-5). The disagreement is often about which part to emphasise in preaching and hope.
19298: Myth: 'Heaven is sitting on clouds playing harps forever.' Correction: harps appear in Revelation's worship scenes (Rev 5:8), but the Bible's final picture is a city, a garden, a river, nations, work and worship on a renewed earth, centred on God's presence. The 'clouds and harps' picture comes mainly from art and cartoons.
19300:
Because hell is an emotional subject, each view is often attacked in a weak form.

About hell in general: 'Satan rules hell and tortures people.' Scripture pictures the devil as a prisoner thrown into the lake of fire, not its king (Rev 20:10, Matt 25:41). The image of Satan as ruler of hell comes largely from later literature and art.

About the debate itself: 'Only liberals question eternal torment.' In fact, conditional immortality and universalism both have early Christian defenders, and conditionalism in particular is now held by many theologically conservative evangelicals. On the other side, 'only harsh fundamentalists believe in eternal torment' is also false; it has been the view of most of the church's most compassionate saints and thinkers.

About Jesus: 'Jesus never talked about hell; Paul invented it' and 'Paul talked about hell constantly' are both wrong. Most of the New Testament's Gehenna sayings come from Jesus (Matt 5:29-30, Matt 23:33). Paul speaks of wrath, death and destruction (Rom 2:5-8, 2 Thess 1:9) but never uses the word Gehenna.

A fair discussion names the strongest texts on every side and admits that each view has passages it must work hard to explain.
19301: The biggest denominations officially teach eternal punishment (for example Catechism of the Catholic Church 1033-1037), but many emphasise the hell of self-exclusion from God more than physical fire. The Church of England's Doctrine Commission report *The Mystery of Salvation* (1995) described hell in terms of final non-being, showing the range within one church (needs verification of exact wording).
19302: Three views of hell compared across eight questions
19304: Is the human soul immortal by nature?
19305: Usually yes (or made so by God)
19306: No; immortality is God's gift in Christ
19307: Views vary; most say humans are made for unending life with God
19310: A punishment whose result (destruction) never ends
19311: Punishment of the coming age; duration open, aimed at correction
19313: Ruin or loss, not ceasing to exist
19314: Literally ceasing to exist after judgment
19315: Destruction of sin and the false self, not of the person
19316: Does anyone remain in hell forever?
19318: No; the lost finally cease to exist
19320: What is the purpose of punishment?
19327: Theophilus, Arnobius; Justin and Irenaeus on debated readings
19328: Clement of Alexandria (debated), Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Isaac the Syrian
19330: Disproportion: endless penalty for finite sin
19333: The unrepentant exist forever under just judgment and separation from God. Historic majority view (Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, Edwards).
19334: Immortality is God's gift; the unrepentant are punished and then finally destroyed. Held by Fudge, Stott (tentatively), Stackhouse and others.
19335: Judgment is real but remedial; God finally reconciles everyone through Christ. Held by Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and today by Talbott, Parry and Hart.
19337: The final goal is the vision of God in heaven.
19338: The final goal is bodily resurrection on a renewed earth where God dwells with his people.
19339: Which of the 'hell' words in your own Bible translation are Sheol, Hades, Gehenna or Tartarus?
19340: Does the same word 'eternal' in Matthew 25:46 have to mean the same thing for life and for punishment?
19341: Is the fire of Gehenna best read literally, symbolically, or both?
19342: How do each view's supporters handle the texts that seem to favour the others?
19343: If heaven is finally on a renewed earth, how should that change how we speak at funerals?
19345: What is Calvinism, where did it come from, who shaped it, what good and harm has it done, and how do both sides read the Bible verses at the centre of the argument?
19346: Calvinism is a way of understanding salvation that puts God's choice first: people are so turned in on themselves by sin that none would turn to God unless God first chose them and changed their hearts, and God's choice does not depend on anything he foresaw in them. It is named after John Calvin (1509–1564), but its core ideas go back to Augustine in the 400s, and it was given its classic five-point shape at the Synod of Dort in 1618–19, long before the acronym TULIP was invented in the early twentieth century. Its admirers credit it with deep assurance, God-centred worship, schools, missions and ideas about limited government; its critics blame it for fatalism, anxious introspection, harshness and the execution of Michael Servetus. Both sides appeal to the Bible: non-Calvinists point to texts where God wants everyone saved and people resist him, Calvinists to texts where God chooses and draws. Most of the argument is not about whether these verses are inspired but about what words like 'all', 'world', 'draw' and 'choose' mean in context, and fair-minded believers have landed on both sides for sixteen centuries.
19347: Calvinism's central claim is that salvation is God's work from start to finish: God chooses, Christ redeems, the Spirit renews, and the believer responds because God has first acted.
19348: The ideas are older than Calvin: Augustine argued them against Pelagius around 411–430; Calvin systematised them; the Synod of Dort (1618–19) defined the 'five points'; the TULIP acronym dates only from about the early 1900s.
19349: Calvinism is not fatalism and not 'hyper-Calvinism': mainstream Calvinists insist God works through means such as preaching, prayer and real human choices, and they offer the gospel freely to everyone.
19350: Its legacy is mixed and argued over: assurance, worship, education, missions and political liberty on one side; Servetus, introspective anxiety, harshness, church splits and the debated use of Reformed theology to defend apartheid on the other.
19351: The Bible debate turns on context and word meaning: 'all' and 'world' (1 Tim 2:4; 1 John 2:2), 'draw' (John 6:44; John 12:32), and whether Romans 9 and Ephesians 1 speak of individuals chosen for salvation or of groups chosen for a role.
19352: Straw men abound on both sides: Calvinists do not think God is a puppeteer who doesn't care, and non-Calvinists do not think people save themselves.
19353: What Calvinism is, in one breath
19354:
At its simplest, Calvinism answers one question: why does one person come to faith and another does not? The Calvinist answer is: because God, for reasons of his own and not because of anything better in the one who believes, chose to give that person a new heart. Faith is a gift (Eph 2:8-9), new birth comes from God and not from human will (John 1:12-13), and those God chose he will certainly bring to glory (Rom 8:29-30).

The main alternatives answer differently. Arminians (after Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609) say God's grace goes before every person and makes faith possible, but each person can accept or resist it, and God chooses those he foresees will believe. Lutherans hold that God alone saves but that those who are lost reject grace by their own fault, and they refuse to reason further into the mystery. Eastern Orthodox Christians speak of 'synergy', human freedom cooperating with grace. Molinists try to combine strong sovereignty with free choice through God's 'middle knowledge'. 'Provisionists' (a recent label in Southern Baptist circles) hold that the gospel itself is God's sufficient means to enable any hearer to respond.

So the argument is not 'God's sovereignty versus human freedom' as if one side denied one of them. Every side believes in both. The disagreement is about how they fit together and which one explains the final difference between belief and unbelief.
19355: Myth: 'Calvinists believe in God's sovereignty; everyone else believes in free will.' In fact Arminians, Lutherans, Catholics and Orthodox all affirm God's sovereignty, and Calvinists affirm that people make real, willing choices. The dispute is over what kind of freedom humans have and what finally decides who believes.
19357:
Pelagius (c. 354–c. 418) was a British-born monk and moral teacher in Rome who was disgusted by lax Christians. He taught that God had given humans everything they needed to obey: Adam's sin set a bad example but did not corrupt human nature, so people could choose good without any special inner grace. His followers, such as Caelestius, pressed the point further.

Augustine of Hippo (354–430), the North African bishop whose *Confessions* tells how he could not free himself from his own desires until God changed him, saw this as a denial of the gospel. In a long series of writings he argued that since Adam all humanity is bound by sin, that the will is free to choose what it loves but cannot love God until grace heals it, that faith itself is God's gift, and that God has chosen some for salvation by sheer mercy. Late in life, in *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* (c. 428–429), he taught that even perseverance to the end is a gift given to the elect.

The church sided with Augustine against Pelagius: a council at Carthage condemned Pelagian teaching in 418 and the Council of Ephesus confirmed the condemnation in 431. But it did not adopt all of Augustine. The Second Council of Orange (529) insisted that even the beginning of faith is grace, yet it also rejected any predestination to evil and said nothing about irresistible grace. Medieval theologians, Catholic and later Protestant, kept arguing over 'how much Augustine'. Calvinism is, in large part, one strong answer to that question.
19358: Myth: 'Anyone who isn't a Calvinist is a Pelagian.' Pelagius denied that people need inner grace to obey God. Arminians, Catholics, Orthodox and Lutherans all reject Pelagianism and teach that no one can come to God without prior grace. Calling them Pelagian is a straw man.
19360:
Profession: lawyer by training, then theologian, preacher, Bible commentator and pastor. Jean Cauvin was born on 10 July 1509 in Noyon, in Picardy, northern France, where his father worked as a legal and financial administrator for the local bishop. He was sent to Paris to study for the church, but his father, after a quarrel with the cathedral clergy, redirected him to law at Orléans and Bourges. There he also absorbed Renaissance humanism, the movement to go back to original sources; his first book (1532) was a commentary on the Roman philosopher Seneca.

Sometime around 1533–34 he was converted to the evangelical cause; he later described the change as sudden and as God subduing a stubborn mind. After his friend Nicolas Cop gave a reform-minded university address in Paris in November 1533, Calvin had to flee. In Basel in 1536 he published the first edition of the *Institutes of the Christian Religion*, a short handbook of Protestant belief with a preface defending persecuted French Protestants to King Francis I. He kept enlarging it until the final Latin edition of 1559 (French 1560).

Passing through Geneva in 1536, he was pressed by the reformer Guillaume Farel to stay. The city's council expelled both men in 1538 in a dispute over church discipline. Calvin spent three happy years in Strasbourg pastoring French refugees, learning from Martin Bucer and marrying Idelette de Bure (1540). Geneva invited him back in 1541, and he stayed until his death on 27 May 1564, preaching several times a week, writing commentaries on most of the Bible, setting up a consistory to oversee morals, founding the Geneva Academy (1559) and training pastors who carried Reformed faith into France, the Netherlands, Scotland and beyond. He was frequently ill, and his only child died in infancy; Idelette died in 1549.

Predestination was important to Calvin but not his organising centre: in the 1559 *Institutes* he placed it under the work of the Holy Spirit and the Christian life (Book 3), treating it as a comfort to believers rather than a starting axiom.
19361: Myth: 'Calvin ruled Geneva as a dictator.' Calvin was a pastor, not a magistrate; he did not become a citizen until 1559, and the city councils often overruled him. He had real moral influence, especially after 1555, but historians describe a negotiated, often tense relationship with the civil authorities rather than a theocracy run by one man.
19363:
Michael Servetus (c. 1509/1511–1553) was a Spanish physician and scholar of real brilliance; he is credited with one of the first European descriptions of the blood's circulation through the lungs. He also rejected the doctrine of the Trinity and infant baptism, which in his century, for Catholics and Protestants alike, were crimes against the state as well as the church. He had corresponded angrily with Calvin for years. In 1553 he was arrested by Catholic authorities in Vienne, France, escaped, and was condemned and burned in effigy there.

In August 1553 he turned up in Geneva and was recognised at a sermon and arrested. Calvin supplied the theological charges and argued against him in the trial. The verdict and sentence belonged to Geneva's Small Council, which first consulted the Reformed churches of Zurich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen; all agreed he should be punished. He was burned alive at Champel on 27 October 1553. Calvin had asked that he be beheaded instead, a less cruel death, but the council refused.

Most Protestant leaders at the time, including the gentle Philip Melanchthon, approved. A minority did not: Sebastian Castellio published a protest in 1554 arguing that killing a man is not defending a doctrine. Calvin defended the execution in print. In 1903 Reformed Christians in Geneva erected an 'expiatory monument' at the site, honouring Calvin while condemning the error of his age. Both halves of the story matter: the execution was not unusual for the sixteenth century, and it was still a grave wrong that Calvin actively supported.
19364: Critics argue Servetus shows what a theology of absolute divine control does when joined to state power; defenders reply that Lutherans, Catholics and Anglicans executed heretics too, so the cause was the shared assumption of Christendom, not Calvinism as such. Most modern Calvinists openly call the execution wrong.
